modules.title: Building Your 3-Month Emergency Fund
modules.summary: The difference between one bad month and a financial catastrophe is having money you can reach in 24 hours. Here is how to build that buffer, and where to keep it.

lessons.title: What an emergency fund is (and is not)
lessons.content:
# What an emergency fund is (and is not)

An **emergency fund** is money you can reach in 24 hours for something you did not plan for, so that one bad month never becomes a financial catastrophe.

## What it is

- **A separate account or wallet** — not the one you shop and pay school fees from.
- **Sized on your essentials, not your salary**: rent, food, transport, school fees, medicine.
- **Reachable in 24 hours.**
- **In your own name**, in Zambia, with you as the only person who can move it.
- **Untouched** unless it is a real emergency.

## What it is NOT

| Not this | Why it fails |
|---|---|
| Your main mobile money wallet | Money in the wallet you spend from gets spent. Two thirds of Zambian adults save through mobile money (65.8%), mostly because cash-out is cheaper than a bank trip, not because it is safer. |
| Your NAPSA pension | NAPSA is not an emergency fund and not a savings account you can draw on. Your 5% buys a future monthly pension; touching it early permanently cuts what you receive. |
| A savings group (chilimba) | The research on Zambian chilimba is blunt: it "does not serve as a safety net in emergencies". Use it for a goal with a date. |
| A fixed deposit you cannot break in a day | Not reachable in 24 hours, so it is not an emergency fund. |
| Money held by a relative | It is their money until they choose otherwise. |
| A promise from somebody | A promise is not a fund. |

## How much: three months of essentials

| Your monthly essentials | Target emergency fund |
|---|---|
| K3,000 | K9,000 |
| K5,000 | K15,000 |
| K8,000 | K24,000 |
| K10,000 | K30,000 |

If K30,000 is out of reach, build in stages: **K1,000 first** (your first month of essentials), then **one month**, then **three**. Do not wait for the full number to start.

## Why three months, and why now

- The Bank of Zambia's FinScope 2025 survey found that **34.9%** of Zambian adults say family, relatives or friends is their main source of emergency money within 30 days. Only **11.1%** say savings. Your country's safety net is your family — a fund turns that luck into a plan.
- The Bank of Zambia also reports that the **real savings rate only turned positive in February 2026**, after a prolonged stretch of negative returns. Money that is not earning is quietly shrinking.

## The inflation test — and the honest answer

Inflation was **6.1% in September 2026**. The Bank of Zambia's August 2026 Monetary Policy Report records a **6-month deposit rate of 7.4%** (June 2026) and a policy rate of **10.75%** from 30 September 2026.

So a 6-month deposit at 7.4% **does** beat 6.1% inflation — but only by about **1.3 percentage points**. That is a thin margin, and two honest conclusions follow:

1. The rate is not the main prize. The **habit** is. Money you move on payday without deciding is worth more than a better rate you never get to.
2. Money in a pocket, a tin or your everyday wallet earns **nothing** while prices rise 6.1% a year. It loses roughly 6% of its buying power every year.

> **What to do this week**
> 1. Write down your real monthly essentials (rent, food, transport, school fees, medicine) and multiply by three.
> 2. Open one separate mobile money wallet or bank savings account in your own name and label it EMERGENCY ONLY.
> 3. Optional: agree with your family who is called first in a crisis, and how much they can cover.

> **Where to check**
> Bank of Zambia — the *Interest Rates and Bank Charges* publication and the Monetary Policy Report for the current deposit rate and the inflation figure.

lessons.title: How to build it from K0 in 6-12 months
lessons.content:
# How to build it from K0 in 6-12 months

The goal is not to save a lot. The goal is to save **the same small amount, automatically, every payday**, long enough that it becomes normal.

## The arithmetic that works: goal divided by paydays left

If your essentials are K5,000 a month, your three-month target is K15,000. Over 12 months that is **K1,250 a month**. If that is more than you can carry, extend the runway rather than break the habit: K15,000 over 18 months is about K833 a month.

| Target | Paydays | Amount per payday |
|---|---|---|
| K6,000 | 12 | K500 |
| K9,000 | 12 | K750 |
| K15,000 | 12 | K1,250 |
| K15,000 | 18 | K833 |
| K15,000 | 24 | K625 |

Round up. The last payday carries the remainder.

## A ladder that survives a bad month

Most salaries do not fail all at once. Step the contribution up as the fund grows:

| Months | Into the fund each month | Running total |
|---|---|---|
| 1-3 | K200 | K600 |
| 4-6 | K300 | K1,500 |
| 7-9 | K400 | K2,700 |
| 10-12 | K500 | K4,200 |

After 12 months you hold K4,200 — close to one full month of essentials — and you have a habit that will carry you to the next stage.

## Payday is the only date that matters

Your PAYE and NHIMA are deducted at source, so net pay lands in one place on one day. Your saving must leave on that day too. Set a standing order, or a scheduled wallet transfer, for the day after payday. If the transfer is automatic, the decision is already made on the days when your judgement is worst.

A bank standing order is cheap: FNB Zambia publishes **K6.00 per payment** for a standard standing order. A hundred kwacha a month for a year is K1,200 and one habit.

## Where to keep it

- **Separate mobile money wallet** — fastest to reach, easiest to start, no minimum balance. This is where most members should start.
- **Bank savings account** — better security and a formal statement for lenders. Some banks charge a monthly fee if you fall below a minimum balance, so read the tariff.
- **Not a long fixed deposit.** A deposit you cannot break inside 24 hours is not an emergency fund. If a 6-month deposit at 7.4% tempts you, remember two things: it beats 6.1% inflation by only about 1.3 points, and ask the bank what happens if you must break it early.

## Four things that quietly destroy emergency funds

1. **Borrowing to build savings.** Do not borrow from the cooperative, a savings group or a "quick cash" app to seed your fund. You would pay interest to earn interest, and you would owe two lenders when the shock arrives. Anything above **48% a year** from a money-lender is unlawful, and compound interest is illegal.
2. **One big payment at Christmas.** A K5,000 Christmas spend wipes out five months of K1,000 saving. Plan the holidays out of your pay, not out of your fund.
3. **Using the fund for a "small" emergency.** A friend who asks for K500 "just this once" is not an emergency for your household.
4. **Never topping it back up.** If you use K2,000 of a K9,000 fund, set a date — 90 days — to restore it.

## The recovery rule

When a real emergency comes: take only what you need, write down what it was, and top the fund back up to target within 90 days. A fund that is used and refilled is working. A fund that is used and never refilled becomes a loan you will repay with interest.

> **What to do this week**
> 1. Set a transfer of K100 — or whatever you can carry without dipping — for the day after your next payday, into a separate wallet labelled EMERGENCY ONLY.
> 2. Write your three-month target on paper, and the date you expect to reach it.
> 3. Optional: check whether your bank or mobile money operator lets you schedule that transfer once, instead of remembering it every month.

> **Where to check**
> Bank of Zambia — the quarterly *Interest Rates and Bank Charges* booklet for deposit rates and standing-order fees, and your own provider's tariff sheet for mobile money.

modules.title: NAPSA & Retirement: How to Maximize Your Benefits
modules.summary: Your NAPSA contributions are not "just a deduction" — they are your retirement. Here is what the 2026 Act changed, and how to build income on top of it.

lessons.title: How NAPSA works (and why your 5% matters)
lessons.content:
# How NAPSA works (and why your 5% matters)

NAPSA is not a deduction you suffer. It is the only retirement income most Zambian civil servants will ever have — and the 2026 law made it better without asking you for extra money.

## The mechanics

- **You contribute 5%** of your gross monthly earnings.
- **Your employer adds a matching 5%** of its own. That half is on top of your pay; it does not reduce your take-home.
- **10% of your pay goes into your pension account** each month, and half of that is free money.
- "Gross earnings" for NAPSA is **wider than basic salary**: basic pay, bonuses, commissions, severance pay, overtime, leave pay and acting allowances. A payslip that computes NAPSA on basic salary alone understates your pension.

## The ceiling, and what it means for you

| Item | 2026 |
|---|---|
| Insurable earnings ceiling | K37,236 per month |
| Maximum employee contribution (5%) | K1,861.80 |
| Maximum employer contribution (5%) | K1,861.80 |
| Combined maximum | K3,723.60 |
| National Average Earnings (the ceiling is 4 times this) | ZMW 9,309 |

Above the ceiling your pension still grows through indexation and investment returns, but no more of your pay goes in. The income above it has to be built elsewhere — the second lesson in this module.

## What the 2026 Act changed

The **National Pension Scheme Act No. 72 of 2026** was assented to on **4 June 2026**. NAPSA's release of 7 August 2026 states the reforms were brought into effect by **Statutory Instrument No. 62 of 2026**, and NAPSA has already paid out under them. The instrument text was not publicly available when this lesson was written, so confirm the current position with NAPSA.

| Change | What it means for you |
|---|---|
| Minimum monthly pension raised from **K1,861 to K2,327** | It is now 25% of National Average Earnings, up from 20%. 17,806 pensioners benefited, and monthly payments rose from K31.8m (June 2026) to K39.6m (July 2026). |
| Income replacement rate improved from **40% to 45%** | Better — but the contribution rate stayed at 10%, split 5% and 5%. |
| **30% near-retirement lump sum** | New. Available from three months before you retire until the day before you retire. |
| **20% pre-retirement lump sum retained** | Still available: 20% of indexed monthly contributions plus accrued interest, one-off, with written consent, below pensionable age, if you have 60 monthly contributions or you are 45. |
| Employer enforcement | The employer must register you within one month of hiring you. Late contributions attract a **10% penalty per month**. |
| Interest-free advance payments | Launched 8 August 2026 for **pensioners**: **K9,137,772.92** disbursed to 565 pensioners within three days; 34,000 were eligible as at 1 August 2026. |

## The 30% is NOT the 20% plus another 30%

This is the most expensive misunderstanding in the 2026 reforms.

- If you have **not** taken the 20%, you may take up to **30%** near retirement.
- If you **already took** the 20%, your near-retirement access is **10%** — 30% in total, not 50%.
- Taking either one **permanently lowers** the pension you receive later, because the balance is recalculated on your residual contributions, and it lowers the minimum-pension floor: to **80%** if you took the 20%, and to **70%** if you took both.

Take a lump sum only after you know your monthly pension first: a lump sum today is worth less than a pension paid every month for the rest of your life.

## When you can claim

| Joining date | Early retirement | Normal retirement | Late retirement |
|---|---|---|---|
| Joined **before 14 August 2015** | 50 | 55 | - |
| Joined **on or after 14 August 2015** | 55 | 60 | 65 |

In every case a pension needs **180 monthly contributions — 15 years**. Not 120. If you have changed jobs, ask NAPSA for your contribution statement: a missing month can cost you the right to a pension altogether.

## How the pension is calculated

- Normal retirement pension = **Average Indexed Monthly Earnings multiplied by (0.001111 times the months of pensionable employment)**.
- Early retirement reduces that by an actuarial deduction, and can never take you below the minimum pension.
- Your average monthly earnings are worked out at claim time and indexed annually against national average earnings.

> **What to do this week**
> 1. Read your payslip and confirm both the 5% employee deduction and the 5% employer contribution appear.
> 2. Write down how many monthly contributions you have made, and compare that number with 180.
> 3. Optional: confirm your nominated beneficiary is correct, and note your joining date (before or after 14 August 2015).

> **Where to check**
> NAPSA — for your contribution statement, benefit projection and the current position on the 20% and 30% lump sums.

lessons.title: How to build retirement income on top of NAPSA
lessons.content:
# How to build retirement income on top of NAPSA

NAPSA's stated income replacement rate is now **45%**. That is the floor, not the plan. The rest of your retirement income has to be built deliberately, years before you stop working.

## Where the other income comes from

| Source | What it does | What to watch |
|---|---|---|
| NAPSA pension | The guaranteed monthly income for life | 180 monthly contributions; a lump sum taken early lowers it permanently |
| Your own savings and deposits | Growth on money you can see | Compare the rate against inflation, not against zero |
| Income-producing assets | Rent from a property, or a business you own | Low liquidity — you cannot sell a plot in 24 hours |
| Continued income | A second career, advisory work, family support | Uncertain; treat it as a bonus, not as a plan |

## The rate test: what actually beats inflation

Inflation was **6.1% in September 2026**. Compare every option against that number, not against zero.

| Option | Rate | As at | Against 6.1% inflation |
|---|---|---|---|
| 6-month deposit (market average) | 7.4% | June 2026 | about +1.3 points |
| Composite Treasury bill yield | 11.5% | June 2026 | about +5.4 points |
| Bank of Zambia policy rate | 10.75% | from 30 September 2026 | a benchmark, not an offer |

The honest reading: a 6-month deposit does beat inflation, but only by about 1.3 points, which is thin. The Treasury-bill yield is more attractive, but it is a **market yield that can change**, and a bill is not cash in your hand. Moving money into the right product on a set date is worth more than the last point of yield.

## Tools you can actually use

- **Patumba**, the money-market fund on Airtel Money and MTN MoMo. Minimum **K1**; tenors of 91, 182, 273 and 365 days and two years. It invests mainly in fixed-term deposits and Treasury bills and aims to track the 365-day Treasury bill rate, but it **does not guarantee a rate upfront**. Ask your operator for the rate on the day you invest.
- **A bank savings account or fixed deposit.** Check the Bank of Zambia's quarterly *Interest Rates and Bank Charges* booklet for what banks are paying, and read your own bank's tariff for monthly fees and minimum balances.
- **A credit union savings account.** One named Zambian credit union advertises **10% a year** on member savings with a minimum balance of K2,500, usable as collateral. One provider is not a market rate — ask for the terms in writing before you rely on it.
- **A savings group (chilimba).** Groups of 4 to 20 members, fixed contributions, a set rotation, and new members joining at the end of the rotation. Good for a goal with a date; the evidence says it does not serve emergencies. Only 13% of savings groups have bank accounts and just 11% use mobile money, which is why a phone ledger matters: the Chilimba and KwachaKash apps, or a bank-run group account such as Access Bank's Tenga (minimum ZMW 100, with automated share-out). The Bank of Zambia's diagnosis of why savings groups fail is poor record keeping, not a shortage of willingness.

## The property route — and its real limit

In Zambia you never own land outright. All land is held from the State on a **renewable 99-year lease** granted by the Lands Commission, and land allocation does not confer ownership. NAPSA itself sells land: River View Park plots in Lusaka are priced from **K460 to K1,771 per square metre** depending on category, with cash payment terms of up to three and six months, and a mortgage facility arranged with Zambia National Building Society.

Property is good long-run retirement income, with two honest warnings. You cannot sell it in 24 hours, and it only produces income if somebody is actually paying rent. Do not count an unsold plot as income.

## The plan that works on a salary

1. **Keep paying your 5%.** It is the only guaranteed income you will have.
2. **Add a private retirement amount each payday** — even K200 — into a product you have already chosen, not one you intend to research later.
3. **Step it up once a year**, taken at your next promotion rather than by cutting something else.
4. **Ask NAPSA for a benefit projection** and write the monthly pension number down. Build the rest of your retirement plan against that number, not against a guess.
5. **Nominate and review your beneficiary** every few years.

> **What to do this week**
> 1. Ask NAPSA for your contribution statement and a benefit projection, and write your projected monthly pension on paper.
> 2. Choose one retirement product — a bank deposit, Patumba, or a credit union account — and open it this month, even if you start with K100.
> 3. Optional: set a recurring reminder for the same date each year to step your private retirement amount up by one increase.

> **Where to check**
> NAPSA for your benefit projection and the lump-sum rules, and the Bank of Zambia for the deposit and Treasury-bill rates quoted here.

modules.title: Banking in Zambia: Hidden Costs & Smart Choices
modules.summary: A bank account is more than a place to keep money. Learn what the banks charge, what the mobile-money levy now costs you, and how to keep more of every kwacha.

lessons.title: Choosing a Zambian bank: the 6 main options compared
lessons.content:
# Choosing a Zambian bank: the 6 main options compared

A bank account is your record, your loan security and your emergency cash. Here is what the banks actually charge.

## Start with the numbers, not the brand

The Bank of Zambia publishes **monthly fees and minimum balances** for every commercial bank in its quarterly *Interest Rates and Bank Charges* publication. As at **31 March 2026** the published retail charges include:

| Bank | Account | Monthly fee | Minimum balance |
|---|---|---|---|
| ZANACO | Current | K100 | K160 |
| ZANACO | Savings | K100 | K100 |
| Standard Chartered | Savings | K200 | K300 |
| FNB | Savings | K300 | K120 (K350 at a branch) |
| Stanbic | Savings | K50 | K105 |
| UBA | Savings | K250 | K500 |

A monthly fee of K50 to K250 is not what should decide your choice. **The charges that hurt are the incident fees.** From FNB Zambia's published pricing guide:

| Charge | Published amount |
|---|---|
| Branch cash withdrawal | K140.00 |
| Other bank's ATM withdrawal | K19.50 (own-bank ATM K8.00) |
| Dishonoured payment (a bounced transaction) | K510.00 |
| Standing order | K6.00 per payment |

Most bank charges punish two things: going to a branch, and a payment bouncing because your balance was short. The Bank of Zambia's table and a bank's own guide describe different products, so **your bank's tariff sheet governs your account.**

## The 6 options, and who each one suits

| Bank | Best for | Watch for |
|---|---|---|
| **ZANACO** | Civil servants paid on a government account | Savings needs a **K350** minimum and allows **one withdrawal a month** at the standard fee; interest is paid twice a year. |
| **Standard Chartered** | A modern app and international transfers | Smart Banking Gold: no minimum balance, ZMW 55 a month. Flexi Cash: ZMW 500 opening balance, ZMW 70 a month. Marathon Savings: ZMW 500 opening, four free debit transactions a month. |
| **FNB** | Strong digital tools and a fixed-deposit ladder | Smart Account K45 a month with a K60 minimum operating balance, waived only at higher tiers. Fixed deposits run from 1 to 60 months, minimum K100. |
| **Stanbic** | A salary account alongside loan products | Retail savings fee K50 with a K105 minimum; compare the loan pricing before you sign. |
| **Access Bank** | A savings circle run by a bank | Tenga Group Savings runs on Tenga Mobile Money with a **ZMW 100** minimum and automated share-out. |
| **UBA** | Banking across Africa | Savings K250 a month with a K500 minimum, one of the highest published. ABSA, by contrast, publishes savings at a K20 monthly fee with a K50 minimum. |

## The rates you are shopping against

| Indicator | Figure | As at |
|---|---|---|
| Bank of Zambia policy rate | 10.75% | from 30 September 2026 |
| Average commercial-bank lending rate | 27.5% | June 2026 |
| Published average salary-backed personal loan rates | 11.00% (Bank of China) to 37.00% (First Alliance) | 31 March 2026 |

Read the middle row carefully. **27.5% is a published average, and it is a ceiling, not today's offer.** The salary-backed figures are averages across borrowers, they exclude fees and insurance, and rates have fallen with the policy rate cuts of 2026. Only one thing tells you what you will pay: **ask your own bank what it would charge you on your own salary, in writing.**

## Choosing well

1. **Where does your salary land?** Keep that account open and in good standing even after you move your savings elsewhere — banks price salary-backed loans on what they can see.
2. **Count your real usage.** Two own-bank ATM withdrawals and one branch visit a month is a different bank from one with a queue every payday.
3. **Check the minimum balance against your real balance.** A minimum you dip below turns into a monthly fee, quietly, every month.

## If something goes wrong

The Bank of Zambia's Customer Service Charter promises that a complaint logged in writing to the Manager-Banking is acknowledged within **two working days** and resolved within **ten working days**. The Bank of Zambia is at Bank Square, Cairo Road, Lusaka (Mon-Fri 08:00 to 14:30), telephone **+260 211 399 300**, email **info@boz.zm**.

FinScope 2025 found **76.2%** of Zambian adults use mobile money but only **30.1%** use a commercial bank. Mobile money is for spending. A bank account is for your record, your emergency money and your future loan.

> **What to do this week**
> 1. Find the monthly fee, the minimum balance and the withdrawal charges on the account you use now, from your bank's own tariff sheet.
> 2. Compare your three most common charges (ATM, branch cash, transfers) against the tables above.
> 3. Optional: if the charges do not add up, ask your bank for the full fee schedule in writing before you decide to move.

> **Where to check**
> Bank of Zambia — the quarterly *Interest Rates and Bank Charges* booklet (latest edition: March 2026) for every bank's published fees, minimum balances and lending rates.

lessons.title: Mobile money: how to use it without losing to fees
lessons.content:
# Mobile money: how to use it without losing to fees

Mobile money is where most Zambian money actually lives. It is fast and cheap for small payments, and the easiest place to lose money to a fee you did not know you were paying.

## First: the levy, and what it is not

From **1 January 2026** the mobile money transaction levy was **increased** — roughly doubled on most bands, and up to 2.8 times on the largest. On a K5,000 transfer the levy rose from K2.00 to K7.50; above K10,000 it rose from K3.60 to K10.00. It is charged on **person-to-person transfers only**, the **sender** pays it, and it sits **on top of** the operator's own fee.

| Amount sent | Levy from 1 January 2026 | Levy from 1 January 2025 |
|---|---|---|
| K0 - 150 | K0.32 | K0.16 |
| Above 150 - 300 | K0.40 | K0.20 |
| Above 300 - 500 | K0.80 | K0.40 |
| Above 500 - 1,000 | K2.00 | K1.00 |
| Above 1,000 - 3,000 | K4.00 | K1.60 |
| Above 3,000 - 5,000 | K7.50 | K2.00 |
| Above 5,000 - 10,000 | K8.00 | K3.00 |
| Above 10,000 | K10.00 | K3.60 |

What the levy is **not**:

- It is **not a tax on your salary**. Nobody deducts it from your payslip.
- It is **not a charge for paying a merchant**. Cash withdrawals and merchant payments are reported as carrying no levy, the better-supported reading of the Act.
- It is **not charged on money you receive**. If your child sends you K500, that is their cost.

ZRA now administers the levy.

## The operator's own fee — and why your tariff sheet counts

Published schedules differ between operators, and sources conflict on the higher cash-out bands. Do not quote a fee from a newspaper or a WhatsApp forward. **Open your operator's published tariff sheet, or read the fee on your phone before you confirm.** An agent must not ask for extra cash on top of the fee already deducted from your wallet.

| | MTN MoMo | Airtel Money |
|---|---|---|
| Send to a registered number, K5 - 150 | Free | K0.58 |
| Send to a registered number, K5,000.01 - 10,000 | K4.00 | K7.00 |
| Cash-out at an agent, K5,000.01 - 10,000 | K70.00 | K60.00 |

**Cash-out is the expensive part**: receiving is free, getting cash into your hand is what costs. And **cross-network costs about three times a same-network send** — on a K5,000 transfer, one published comparison put a same-network send at K10.50 and a cross-network send at K37.50 on MTN.

Sending to a number that is **not registered** on that network costs several times more. Check the person has a wallet first.

## Your limits, and why to upgrade early

| Wallet tier | Daily limit | Maximum balance | What you need |
|---|---|---|---|
| MTN Individual Tier 1 | K20,000 | K100,000 | NRC (passport for foreigners) |
| MTN Individual Tier 2 | K100,000 | K500,000 | Tier 1 documents, proof of residence and an employer or civic referral |
| Airtel Platinum Tier 2 | K100,000 | K500,000 | as above |

A civil servant can supply every Tier 2 item. Upgrade before you need it, not in the week you need K80,000. No published monthly cap for individual wallets was found.

## Four mistakes that cost money

1. **Withdrawing small amounts often.** The fee is the same K2.50 whether you take K50 or K500. Withdraw once a week, in a planned amount.
2. **Borrowing from the wallet.** A mobile-money loan is not a small loan. Ask for the **total you will repay** and the **number of instalments**, then divide. If the lender will not say, walk away.
3. **Trusting a number you were given.** SIM-swap fraud takes over a phone number so that your PIN resets land with the fraudster. ZICTA's rules now require an ID document, a facial photo and identity-system validation before a SIM is activated, 
4. **Ignoring an unfamiliar transaction.** If money leaves your wallet without your instruction, call your operator immediately, then complain to the Bank of Zambia. Under MTN's terms, until the operator receives your notice of a lost phone or suspected PIN compromise, they remain authorised to process requests made with your PIN.

## If your phone is stolen

1. Call your operator's fraud line at once and suspend the wallet. MTN: **8787**, WhatsApp **683008787**, toll-free **111**.
2. Call your bank, freeze linked accounts, and change every PIN: mobile money, bank, email.
3. Review recent transactions, keep the references, and report to the Bank of Zambia if money was taken: **+260 211 399 300**, info@boz.zm, Bank Square, Cairo Road, Lusaka (Mon-Fri 08:00 to 14:30).

> **What to do this week**
> 1. Open your operator's published tariff sheet and write down the fee you pay for your two most common transactions.
> 2. Move your emergency money into a separate wallet, and set the transfer that funds it each payday.
> 3. Optional: check how many SIM cards are registered against your National Registration Card, and close any that are not yours.

> **Where to check**
> Your mobile money operator (MTN MoMo or Airtel Money) for its current published tariff sheet, and the Bank of Zambia for provider complaints.
